THE HERALDRY OF PSI UPSILON
By Clayton W. Butterfield, Pi '11
Just as the various divisions of the
army are
today identified by the in
signia on their equipment, or on the
unifonns of the men, so in the early
ages various tribes and warriors
could be identified by the emblems
and symbols which served as their
particular marks of distinction.
Not only did a tribe have its dis
tinctive identifying mark, but famiHes, too, used emblems to show their
hneage or
allegiance. In the days of
feudalism, a
family who gave alle
giance to a certain feudal lord had a
coat-of-arms which was in certain
details similar to the coat-of-arms of
the family to whom support was
given; but, naturally, the shield was
suflBciently changed so as to indicate
difference in station, etc.
The Greeks and Romans assigned
various emblems to individuals and
to their deities.
Certain emblems were
generally
used in English Heraldry to indicate
whether a 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, etc.,
son of a
family was the bearer of
arms.
In Biblical history, every man
among the Children of Israel was or
dered to pitch his camp by his own
standard�no doubt an individual
sign or emblem.
Various explanations are
given to
the origin of the various units which
make up a coat-of-arms. The early
warriors are said to have painted
their shields or covered them with
metal or furs so that they might
readily be identified or
distinguished
in battle, particularly when the war
riors were in their coats of mail.
The idea is also given credence
that when a warrior returned from a
battle, he hung his shield on the wall
or
placed it on a
big chair-like rack
in the great hall, and above it
placed his helmet. Sometimes a hel
met was decorated with the colors
and ribbons of the warrior's lady
fair. A warrior's coat-of-arms was in
reality a
picturization of his shield
with his decorated helmet above it.
There was also the custom of at
taching to the helmet some
particu
lar emblem to
identify the individ
ual, probably just in case he lost his
shield in battle and still retained his
head, and helmet.
It is also said that the warrior,
when reHeving himself of his shield
and helmet, upon return from an en713

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
gagement, would hang his cloak be
side his shield or
possibly throw it
over the helmet, thus originating the
"mantling" or
flowing decorations
that appear so
frequently above and
around the shield of a coat-of-arms.
Animals are often shown support
ing either side of a shield, and their
use, no doubt, can be traced back to
the time of the tournaments when
knights and esquires had pages or
attendants who were masked to rep
resent animals or
imaginary crea
tures, and who guarded their mas
ter's shield and armor when not in
use.
The motto used ordinarily with a
coat-of-arms is no doubt an out
growth of the war
cry, and in later
days became a statement or indica
tion of some characteristic of the
family or an ideal or ambition. Fre
quently, it had reference to some
achievement and, occasionally, a
similarity or reference to the family
name.
When heraldic emblems were first
used, there was little or no definite
scheme for the adoption or
arrange
ment of the symbols. Later, in vari
ous countries, there were certain
The Arms of the Fraternity
legislative enactments which brought
heraldry and the use of heraldic de
vices to a
systematic and scientific
basis. The color schemes, designs,
symbols, metals and furs used on the
shields, were
originally purported to
suggest deeds of valor, ideals or aims
or
allegiance to some other family.
These legislative enactments
pro
vided clearly as to certain details.
In England, for instance, the rul
ings were established that hehnets
were of four types: 1st, the sov
ereigns', shown full face with six pro
tecting bars�this helmet was crim
son, lined with gold; 2nd, the nobles',
which bore silver helmets of five
bars facing three quarters to the
front, and were adorned with gold;
3rd, the knights'�helmets of steel
with silver ornaments shown full
front view with visor open; and 4th,
the gentlemen's or
esquires'�a steel
helmet in profile with visor closed.
In this way, the details of the coatof-arms gave information readily con
cerning the bearer, his rank, his al
legiance, accomphshments and aims,
In addition to being used by famiTheta Chapter

THE HE
hes and individuals down through
the years, armorial bearings came to
be used by cities and towns as their
oflBcial seals, until, in later years,
states, corporations, guilds, legal or
ganizations, hotels and clubs came
to use heraldic devices quite gener
ally.
This rather popular custom is no
doubt partially due to the fact that
the shield in its various forms makes
an attractive device for indicating a
service offered, and partially due to
a certain pride in
ancestry.
In America, most state and college
seals bear evidence of having their
origin in some historic arms or in
some detail, evidence of the ancient
heraldic science.
Today, the use of armorial bearings
which most nearly conforms to the
historic and established principles of
olden times has been developed by
various college fraternities.
Most fraternities have but one coatof-arms used by the fraternity in
general, with no
special emblems or
symbols for the various chapters.
Only a few have a
system of employDelta Chapter
R A L D R Y
ing one national coat-of-arms and a
similar yet distinctive device for each
chapter. Among these few are. Delta
Kappa Epsilon-Beta Theta Pi�and
our own Psi Upsilon.
In the year 1892, Brothers Albert
P. Jacobs, Phi '73, Karl P. Harring
ton, Xi '82, and George B. Penny,
Chi '85, acting as a Psi Upsilon Her
aldry Committee, prepared and pre
sented a
report proposing the system
of heraldry which was
adopted by
our
fraternity in convention of 1894.
This system is so
simple, so uniform,
and the principles of early heraldry
are followed so well and so
pleas
ingly, it is evident that those "elder
brothers" took their assignments seri
ously and performed their work for
the fraternity with great care, and
with a
thorough knowledge of the
subject.
The following is quoted from the
report submitted by the original Her
aldry Committee to the 1892 Psi Up
silon Convention:
The need of a uniform system of He
raldic representation has long been recog
nized by those members who have been
Beta Chapter

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
called upon to supervise the ornamenta
tion of Chapter Houses, the decoration of
lodge rooms, the printing of Psi U publi
cations, and the illustration of chapter
lists in College annuals. Considerable sums
of money have been wasted in procuring
costly engravings that for the most part
lack spirit, dignity and appropriateness�
that are
Heraldically incorrect, and that
are soon laid aside because they mean
nothing. Besides, these engravings are too
intricate for reproduction in mural decorat
ing, and when one seeks to ornament a
ballroom or dining hall with the emblems
of the fraternity or of the chapters, they
give httle aid. It is obvious that a correct
and significant system of Heraldry could
be employed with great effectiveness in
ritual work. We believe that the Fraternity
would be benefited by the adoption of a
dignified and consistent series of coats-ofarms, reproducing in proper Heraldic form
and position the historic emblems of the
Order and of its several branches. The
ancient symbols upon our
badge, and the
pecuUar emblems adopted by the various
chapters, furnish the material for a com
plete and satisfactory set of armorial de
signs. This Committee has sought to
utilize the old insignia rather than to
introduce new
bearings; it has aimed at
simplicity and effectiveness; and it has en
deavored to present a scheme that has at
once an outward significance, and, to the
initiated�a
"deeper meaning" which may
be fully elaborated and explained in the
ritual.
Sigma Chapter
The recommendations in this re
port were
approved and adopted at
the National Convention two years
later, and so, in 1894, the Coats-ofArms of Psi Upsilon came into ex
istence.
The Coats-of-Arms of the various
chapters all have a
similarity read
ily noticed by comparison. There is
a consistent scheme which would
have been impossible had each chap
ter used some device without thought
of the common spirit and identity
of the other chapters. The shields
are uniform size and shape; the owl
for the crest of each; the chapter
mottoes also on uniform scrolls; the
ancient emblems of our Fraternity
appear on each shield together with
other symbols appropriate for each
chapter.
The mottoes of the chapter Coatsof-Arms begin with the characteristic
letter of the chapter, and in most
cases have reference in meaning to
the symbols�or to the secret watch
word of that chapter.
The original Psi Upsilon Heraldry
Committee went on further in their
Gamma Chapter

report to the National Convention in
1892 as follows:
"The subject naturally divides itself into
five divisions:
(a). The Arms of the Fraternity.
(b). The Seal of the Executive Coun
cil.
(c). Seals of Alumni Association.
(d). Arms of the several Chapters.
(e). The Flag of the Fraternity.
These will be developed in their order.
"(a). The Arms of the Fraternity. The
committee recommends a black shield
bearing hands and letters of gold as in
our
badge, around which emblems, runs
what is known as a double tressure flory
counter flory, of silver."
The "double treasure" alludes to
the "tie that binds" the secrets, ideals
and aims of the Fraternity.
"The black shield is chosen not only be
cause it is more effective than any other
hue in hne engraving (which wiU be the
chief use of the coat-of-arms ) , but also be
cause it is the background of the badge.
Boyesen's 'St�ir-Song', it will be remem
bered, refers to the 'sable shield' and the
"hands of flame.'
"The crest here recommended consists
of an owl surmounting Roman fasces."
This possibly needs no
explanation, but to
refresh our memories, the owl was as
signed by the Greeks to Pallas Athena as
an emblem of her supernal wisdom, and
by the Romans to Minerva, Goddess of
Wisdom. The fasces, which the owl sur
mounts, was a term given a bundle of elm
sticks or branches boimd together with
leather thongs or lashes, and containing an
ax with blade projecting from the side.
These were carried by lectors (pubhc oflBcers
attending Roman Magistrates), and
were
symbols of power.

of the shield, and by a
yellow one at the
left, from which, imited below the shield,
depends by a
ring a Psi Upsilon badge.

"(d). Arms of the several Chapters. In
recommending a
general scheme for chap
ter coats-of-arms, we are not unmindful of
the fact that each chapter has the right to
adopt its own
design, except so far as the
use of the letters and symbols of the Fra
ternity is concerned. We do not advise the
Convention to encroach in the least degree
upon the individual privileges of any branch
of our brotherhood. It is, however, ap
parent, diat a consistent and harmonious

own
jeweler or
engraver; and it must be
clear that a common

identity

We believe that the plan which we advise
the Fraternity to recommend to its chap

approval. In
fact, it is so natural and so
simple, that it
practically excludes every other scheme,
and we are confident that it will bear the
test of time and become more and more

"The proposed system of chapter coatsof-arms involves three principal features:
(1) Identity of crest; (2) Mottoes framed
on a uniform plan; and, (3) Shields, each
combining, in accordance with a
carefully
arranged schedule, the principal emblems

Kappa Chapter
hands) with the peculiar emblem of the

"We propose diat the shields shall be
alternately silver and gold, the first, third,
fifth, etc., chapters in the order of institu
tion having silver shields, and the second,
fourth, sixth, etc., chapters having gold
shields. The chapter emblem to be col
ored as
suggested by its nature or, in some
cases, by the college color. Thus, the chev

Gamma should be purple on a white
ground, the torch of Lambda should be

"To indicate the connection of the chap

propose to in

The National Coat-of-Arms and
most of all the Chapter Coat-of-Arms
were
designed by Brother Albert P.
Jacobs, Phi '73, with the help of the
other members of his original com
mittee.
There is every evidence that dur
ing the several years following the
estabhshment of the Psi Upsilon sys
tem of heraldry, the adoption of the
national coat-of-arms and the variXi Chapter

ous

Although the original committee's
report was on file and records of the
national bearings and the coats-ofarms of the 21 Chapters are
complete
in detail, there appears to be no rec
ord of any standing committee who

In 1921, the Executive Council
appointed the writer to act as a
Heraldry Committee Chairman, and
requested that he design suitable
coats-of-arms for the additional
Chapters that had been and were to
be established in later years. Assist
ance in this work was
readily ob
tained by enlisting the good services
of Brothers J. I. Chamberlain�Beta
'95; Wm. T. Aldrich-Sigma '01 and
H. G. Coddington-Pi '86.
The designing of coats-of-arms for
the Nu, Epsilon, Omicron, Delta
Delta, Epsilon Phi and Zeta Zeta was
Alpha Chapter

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
therefore accomplished, although it
involved years of intermittent corre
spondence with these Chapters to
finally decide on suitable emblems,
mottoes and general designs, in order
to make each Chapter coat-of-arms
conform precisely to the rules of the
early heraldic devices and the Psi U
system of Heraldry.
When your present committee un
dertook the task, in addition to the
21 coats-of-arms already adopted, it
was found that the Rho and the
Theta Theta had also decided upon
their Chapter coat-of-arms, which
were, with the exception of minor
details in the case of Theta Theta
(the proportions of the shield and
scroll and lettering on the scroll did
not conform to the uniform design
for all Chapters), in strict accord
with the original system.
Psi Upsilon now has its heraldic
devices for each and every Chapter
completely designed, approved and
in use, and it is interesting to con
sider the emblems, and mottoes of
these various coats-of-arms. Whenwe
stop to consider the emblem or
symUpsilon Chapter

public motto of each Chapter, we
can
readily see their reference to
some incident in the early years of

aims, or a reference to the Chapter's
secret watchword or secret motto.
The Theta coat-of-arms�the bear

its emblem a rock with the waves of
the sea
pounding against it. This em

The emblem of the Theta as rec

watchword better than any other

this emblem was eliminated and the
rock chosen before the Theta Coatof-Arms was
definitely adopted.
